items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: We stayed at a hotel in Wiley Avenue and ate in a big restaurant near by, which was owned by a fellow named Gus Greenly.

ctx.x: The car had inside and outside rims and when one blew out, the outside rim would jump off, it would go rolling ten yards away from the car. The inside rim would hit against the body of the car with such force that it sounded as though a bomb had exploded. So much dust would come out up from the force of the rim hitting against the car that it looked like a foggy day in London town. But it didn't smell like that. There must have been dust in that wagon that was there from the coffin of the first person that died…

We started going to Pittsburg, Pennsylvania and playing dances there and in Duquesne and mining towns not too far from Pittsburg. In most large cities or I should say in every large city in the country, there was wide open vice. Bootleg whisky, home brew, gambling and prostitution. Pittsburgh was jumping and Wiley Avenue was the main drag for the pimps, musicians and hustlers. We stayed at a hotel in Wiley Avenue and ate in a big restaurant near by, which was owned by a fellow named Gus Greenly.

Gus had known the Scott orchestra before I joined it and he was very fond of Lloyd, Cecil and the other members that had been and those that were now with the orchestra. Gus also had a gambling place next door to the restaurant and there was always a thousand dollars in silver dollar pieces stacked on the crap shooting table. Lloyd Scott was the only one in the orchestra that liked to gamble. He very seldom won anything.
